Can you use an iPad as a family calendar display?

Yes. An iPad can work very well as a shared family calendar display, especially if you already own one. You can show everyone's schedules, add appointments, color-code family members, and keep events synchronized with their phones.

The important distinction is that a shared calendar app is not necessarily a complete household dashboard.

A dedicated family calendar, such as a Skylight Calendar or a Hearth Display, is designed to be a central place for family organization. An iPad can replicate much of that experience, but the right setup depends on whether you want a simple calendar or a display that also handles chores, routines, meal planning, and other household information.

An iPad is particularly attractive when you want to reuse existing hardware and avoid paying for a second screen.

2. What the different setups look like

Apple Calendar — simplest for Apple families

Native iPad app with shared iCloud calendars, multiple calendar colors, and event editing. Apple confirms that invited iCloud users can receive viewing or editing permission. 
Apple Support (IS)

Best when the iPad will mainly show appointments and family events.

Google Calendar — best for mixed devices

Shared calendars with configurable permissions, accessible from iPads, iPhones, Android phones, and browsers. Google officially supports synchronizing Google events with Apple's Calendar app. 
Google Calendar Help
+1

Best when several people need to add and change events from their own phones.

DAKboard — best dashboard-style alternative

A customizable screen that can combine calendar information with weather, photographs, and other widgets. It is more suitable for glanceable household information than a conventional calendar app.

Best for a kitchen or hallway screen viewed throughout the day.

Cozi Family Organizer — best for shared planning

Combines a family calendar with shopping lists, to-do lists, and meal-planning tools. Its primary experience is an organizer that family members interact with, rather than a permanently displayed dashboard.

Best when household planning matters as much as seeing the schedule.

4. Sync limitations: what actually works?

Apple confirms that iCloud shared calendars can grant editing rights, while public calendar subscriptions are read-only. Google confirms that its events can sync to Apple Calendar. 
Apple Support (IS)
+2

There are three practical gotchas.

First, display refresh is not instant synchronization. DAKboard's published plan comparison specifies calendar refresh intervals of 60 minutes on Free, 30 minutes on Essential, and 15 minutes on Plus. A successfully updated Google event might therefore take time to appear on the display. 
dakboard.com

Second, permissions matter. If you connect a calendar that you can only view, the iPad won't gain editing rights just because it displays that calendar. Google's sharing controls distinguish between seeing event details and making changes. 
Google Calendar Help

Third, even dedicated hardware has limits. Skylight's official documentation distinguishes two-way Google/iCloud connections from one-way Outlook, Yahoo, Cozi, and other connections. A dedicated screen doesn't guarantee universal two-way synchronization. 
Skylight Support

5. How I'd set up an existing iPad

1. Choose one primary calendar system

Use iCloud for an Apple-only family, or Google Calendar for a mixed-device family. Create a shared family calendar and grant editing access to the people who need it.

2. Choose the screen experience

Start with the native calendar app. If it feels too much like a personal productivity app, try DAKboard's family display on the iPad. DAKboard explicitly supports using an existing iPad, including its TouchHub interface. 
dakboard.com

3. Configure the iPad as a shared display

Put it on a stable stand or suitable mount, provide reliable power, adjust Auto-Lock, and use Guided Access to restrict it to the calendar or dashboard. Apple officially documents both settings. 
Apple Support (IE)
+1

4. Protect private information

Prefer a dedicated household account or narrowly shared family calendar over signing the communal iPad into someone's entire personal account. Avoid showing confidential work appointments, private notifications, or personal email.

5. Test real synchronization

Add an event on one family member's phone, edit it on another, and check the iPad. Then test whether changes made on the iPad reach the phones. This confirms the actual behavior of your chosen setup.

For a permanently powered iPad, consider screen brightness, battery heat, cable placement, and the possibility of image retention. An iPad can serve as a stationary display, but it wasn't designed exclusively for that role.

6. My recommendation

Best starting point: existing iPad + Google or Apple Calendar

Low cost

No new hardware, native editing, and straightforward sharing. Try it for a week before paying for anything.

Best replacement for a dedicated family display: iPad + DAKboard

The stronger choice if you want a glanceable household dashboard with calendar, weather, chores, and other information. Its free tier supports two calendars; advanced layouts and chores can require a paid plan. 
dakboard.com
+1

Choose dedicated hardware only when the display itself matters

Consider it if you want a larger, permanently mounted, purpose-built screen and prefer an integrated product over maintaining an iPad setup.

Bottom line: I would reuse the iPad first. The calendar synchronization is entirely achievable, and DAKboard makes a household-style interface possible without buying another screen. The biggest differences are display size, refresh behavior, editing workflow, and how much household functionality you want beyond appointments.
